rationale: Round 0 compiled and ran correctly with no reported failures, so this round raises obfuscation pressure across all seven passes to improve reverse-engineering resistance. FLA and IGV get the highest SecurityGain because the profile is dominated by small hot numeric kernels (flops, fbench, whetstone, matmul) where control-flow flattening and global-variable indirection destroy per-function structure cheaply; their RuntimeCost weights stay moderate so the selector avoids flattening the innermost FP loops. SUB is pushed hardest on DiversityGain since it is nearly free at runtime and size and preserves FP semantics, making it safe to apply broadly across the many small kernels. SPLIT is enabled as a cheap structural diversifier for the longer functions (ReedSolomon, oourafft, richards) with low cost penalties. BCF and IBR keep strong security weights but slightly higher RuntimeCost/SizeCost penalties to limit bloat in the benchmark's hot loops. ICALL and IGV carry the highest CorrectnessRisk weights (0.30/0.35) because indirect calls and global variable encoding are the passes most likely to break pointer-heavy C code, letting the selector skip them where features indicate risk. Overall correctness risk stays low enough that a working round-0 build should remain correct while coverage and diversity increase substantially.
